mainEntity.name: Why is my backyard less private in the winter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the screening you had was deciduous foliage, and it leaves. Oakland County's median first fall frost falls in the first week of November, and most maples are bare by then. Add lower sun angles that light up interiors in the late afternoon, and a yard that felt enclosed in July reads as open by Thanksgiving. Pin oaks and some red oaks hold their leaves through winter, which is why a few neighborhoods keep their screening longer than others.

mainEntity.name: Does a 6-foot fence block a neighbor's second-story window?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A 6-foot fence blocks ground-level sightlines from flat ground, but from a second-story window at 14 feet nearly the whole yard is visible. From a 3-foot deck the ground beyond about 16 feet past the fence is visible. Above-fence screening — Green Giant arborvitae, a pergola, or a screen panel — is the only fix that does not require a height variance you will not get.

mainEntity.name: Why does my cedar fence have gaps now that it's cold?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wood shrinks as it dries, mostly across the width of the board. Western redcedar shrinks about 5 percent from green to oven-dry, which is roughly a sixth of an inch on a 5.5-inch picket; southern pine shrinks more, closer to a quarter inch. A side-by-side fence butted tight in June opens thin gaps by January as heated air dries the boards. It is not a defect, and board-on-board construction prevents it by overlapping the seams.

mainEntity.name: Is board-on-board worth the extra cost for privacy?

acceptedAnswer.text: If privacy is the actual goal, yes. Board-on-board overlaps the pickets so the seams are covered and stay covered as the wood moves, and both faces look finished. It uses noticeably more cedar per foot than a side-by-side fence, but the labor is comparable, so the premium is material rather than difficulty. Shadowbox looks similar but is deliberately semi-private and lets air and sightlines through.

mainEntity.name: Do arborvitae lose their leaves in winter, and how close should I plant them?

acceptedAnswer.text: Arborvitae are evergreen and keep their foliage year-round, which is exactly why they work as above-fence screening. Plant Emerald Green 3 to 4 feet on center for a hedge; plant Green Giant 5 to 6 feet on center for a taller, faster screen. Keep 2 to 3 feet of clearance from a wood fence so air moves and the boards can be inspected and restained. Expect about three years before a new screen is genuinely private.

mainEntity.name: Can you install a wood fence in November in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, yes, until the ground freezes hard — often late November, sometimes early December if snow insulates the soil. Posts still need to reach below Michigan's 42-inch frost depth, so the work does not get easier as the season closes. Staining should wait for spring, when temperatures hold above 50 degrees long enough for the finish to cure.

mainEntity.name: Does snow make a fence effectively shorter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in practice. A settled snowpack of 12 to 24 inches raises the effective ground line, buries the bottom rail, and lets a dog or a person stand higher than they could in summer. That is why we mark posts with tall stakes, keep a snow storage strip clear of plantings, and clear packed snow away from the bottom rail after big storms.

mainEntity.name: Does a hot tub need a code-compliant privacy barrier?

acceptedAnswer.text: A spa needs a barrier under ISPSC Section 305: at least 48 inches above grade, no opening that passes a 4-inch sphere, no more than a 2-inch gap at the bottom, a self-closing and self-latching gate, and a barrier at least 20 inches from the water's edge. A spa with a lockable ASTM F1346 safety cover is exempt from the barrier requirement, but not from needing privacy. In our experience the inspection fails on gate hardware far more often than on fence height.
